title: The Plain Sense: The Reformers, the Press and the Bible in Every Hand
standfirst: The Reformation and the Open Bible
subtitle: Gutenberg's press, the humanist return to the sources, Erasmus's Greek Testament, Luther's grammatical sense and his German Bible, Tyndale's English, Calvin's brevity, sola scriptura in its own terms, the answer at Trent, and the individual reader the age left behind.

sections.title: When the Bible Became a Book You Owned
sections.body:
Before the middle of the fifteenth century, most Christians met the Bible as something heard rather than held. It came to them in the Latin of the Mass, in the painted walls and windows of the parish church, in the cycle of feasts and fasts, and in sermons that retold its stories inside the church's teaching. A complete manuscript Bible cost a small fortune and many months of a scribe's labor, and it lived in monasteries, cathedrals and the libraries of the wealthy. The ordinary believer did not so much read Scripture as inhabit it, through a community that read it on his behalf.

Within two centuries that arrangement had broken apart. By 1650 a farmer in England, a burgher in Zurich or a weaver's wife in Saxony might own a Bible in their own tongue, read it at their own table, and argue with the pastor about what it said. The causes were several and they reinforced one another: a machine that multiplied texts, a scholarly movement that wanted the oldest texts, and a theological revolution that staked the reform of the church on what those texts plainly meant. Together they produced the most consequential change in how Christians read Scripture since the canon was settled.

This essay is about that change, and it is written by someone who stands at its far end. I pastor a Baptist church. My tradition took the Reformation's confidence in the open Bible and pressed it further than Luther or Calvin ever meant it to go, until the individual conscience with a Bible in hand could seem to need no one else at all. Much of what follows is gain, and I will defend it. Some of it is a debt we have not yet paid. Both belong to the story, because the reading habits this age created are the ones most Protestants still mistake for the way a Bible is simply read.

sections.title: Gutenberg and the Multiplied Page
sections.body:
The first major book printed in Europe with movable metal type was a Bible. Johann Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz completed it around 1455, a Latin Vulgate set in two columns of forty-two lines, and the surviving copies are still among the most beautiful books ever made. It is worth noticing what it was not. It was not a vernacular Bible, and it was not a cheap one. Gutenberg's aim was more modest than the revolution that followed: to produce, more quickly and more uniformly, the book the church already used.

But a technology does not stay inside its inventor's intentions. Within half a century presses were at work in more than two hundred European towns, and the cost of a book fell steeply. Print did several things at once that manuscript culture could not. It fixed a text, so that readers in different cities could point to the same words on the same page. It allowed an error to be corrected across a whole edition rather than copied forward one manuscript at a time. It made comparison possible, since a scholar could lay editions side by side and ask which reading was older. And it made texts portable, private and silent in a way they had rarely been.

The historian Elizabeth Eisenstein argued that the press was itself an agent of change rather than merely a faster pen, and her case has been debated and qualified ever since. The qualification matters. Print did not create the Reformation, and for most people the Bible remained for generations a book read aloud to them, since literacy rose slowly and unevenly. Yet without the press, Luther's protest of 1517 might have stayed one more local quarrel in a Saxon university town. With it, his writings were read across the German lands within weeks. The press decided nothing about what Christians would believe; it decided how fast, and how far, the argument would travel.

sections.title: Erasmus and the Return to the Sources
sections.body:
The humanists of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries had a watchword, ad fontes, back to the sources. They meant it first of the classics: read Cicero in his own Latin, not in a digest. The principle soon reached the Bible. If the best way to know an ancient author was to read him in his own language and from the best manuscripts, then the church's Latin Vulgate was a translation, venerable but secondary, and the Greek of the apostles stood behind it.

Lorenzo Valla had already shown what that kind of attention could do. Around 1440 he demonstrated from its Latin that the Donation of Constantine, a document on which papal claims to temporal power partly rested, could not have been written in the fourth century. His notes comparing the Vulgate with the Greek New Testament lay in manuscript until Erasmus of Rotterdam found them and published them in 1505. Eleven years later, in 1516, Erasmus brought out at Basel, through the printer Johann Froben, the first published Greek New Testament, with his own Latin translation and annotations.

The edition was hurried, and its Greek rested on a handful of late manuscripts. Its importance lay elsewhere. It told the reader that the Vulgate could be checked and corrected. Where the Latin of Matthew 4:17 had Jesus call his hearers to do penance, the Greek could be read as a summons to repent, to turn the whole mind, and a sacramental system seemed to hang on the difference. Erasmus remained a Catholic until his death in 1536, and he wanted a reformed, learned and gentle Christianity, not a divided one. In his prefaces he hoped that the Scriptures would be translated so that the farmer at his plough and the weaver at his loom might know them. He did not foresee what that hope would set loose, and he spent his later years quarrelling with the man who loosed it.

sections.title: Luther and the Grammatical Sense
sections.body:
Medieval exegesis worked with a fourfold sense of Scripture, often called the quadriga. Beyond the literal sense, which told what happened, a passage could carry an allegorical sense concerning Christ and the church, a tropological sense concerning the conduct of the soul, and an anagogical sense concerning the last things. Jerusalem could be at once a city in Judea, the church, the faithful soul and the heavenly city. At its best this was a disciplined reading of the whole canon as one witness to Christ. At its worst it let an interpreter find almost anything anywhere, and whoever held the keys of interpretation held the text.

Martin Luther was formed in this method and used it as a young professor at Wittenberg. Across his early lectures on the Psalms and on Romans he moved away from it toward what he called the grammatical or literal sense, the meaning the words bear in their own language and setting. He did not stop reading the Old Testament as testimony to Christ; he believed the plain sense of the Psalms already spoke of him. What he refused was the multiplication of hidden meanings as a way of escaping what a text actually said. Against Erasmus, in The Bondage of the Will of 1525, he insisted on the clarity of Scripture: its central matter, Christ crucified and risen, was not obscure, whatever difficulties remained in particular words.

Hidden at the Wartburg after his condemnation at the Diet of Worms in 1521, he translated the New Testament into German from Erasmus's Greek in about eleven weeks. It appeared in September 1522 and its first printing sold quickly. By his own account he listened to the mother in the house, the children in the street and the common man in the market, so that his German would sound like German. A people learned to hear the apostles in the speech of their own kitchens.

sections.title: Tyndale and the Price of a Translation
sections.body:
In England the cost of the open Bible was paid in blood. Under the Constitutions of Oxford, issued in 1409 against the followers of John Wycliffe, it was forbidden to translate Scripture into English, or to read such a translation, without a bishop's license. William Tyndale, an Oxford-trained scholar with superb Greek, sought the patronage of Cuthbert Tunstall, bishop of London, for a translation of the New Testament and was refused. He left for the continent, and after a first printing at Cologne was interrupted, his English New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled home in merchants' cargoes. Tunstall had copies bought up and burned at St Paul's.

The quarrel was about words as much as access. Tyndale rendered the Greek ekklesia as congregation rather than church, presbyteros as elder rather than priest, the call to metanoia as repent rather than do penance, and agape as love rather than charity. Thomas More, in his Dialogue Concerning Heresies of 1529, saw at once what was at stake: each choice moved authority away from the institution and toward the gathered people and the inward turn of the heart. More was right about the theological freight, whatever one thinks of what he did about it. Translation is never neutral, and Tyndale knew it.

John Foxe's martyrology records that Tyndale once told a learned opponent he would make the boy who drives the plough know more of the Scripture than he did. Whatever the exact words, the ambition was real. Betrayed in Antwerp, Tyndale was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde in 1536. Within three years an English Bible built heavily on his work had been ordered into every parish church, and much of his phrasing passed through the Geneva Bible of 1560 into the King James Version of 1611. Most English-speaking Christians who have quoted the New Testament have quoted Tyndale without knowing his name.

sections.title: Calvin's Brevity and the Discipline of the Text
sections.body:
If Luther gave the plain sense its fire, John Calvin gave it its method. Trained in law and humanist letters before his conversion, he brought to Scripture the habits of a classical philologist: attention to grammar, to historical setting, to the author's purpose in writing. In 1540 he published his commentary on Romans, and in its dedicatory letter to the Basel scholar Simon Grynaeus he set out his ideal. The chief virtue of an interpreter, he argued, is lucid brevity, and almost his only task is to lay open the mind of the writer he has undertaken to explain. To lead readers away from the author's meaning is to wander from the interpreter's whole purpose.

Calvin kept that rule with a severity that can still surprise. He declined to treat the plural Hebrew name for God in the first verse of Genesis as proof of the Trinity, because he did not think the text, read in its own setting, would bear the weight, and a Lutheran critic later accused him of Judaizing for such restraint. Over the following two decades he wrote commentaries on most of the Bible and preached through whole books in Geneva several times a week. The Institutes of the Christian Religion, first published in 1536 and enlarged until 1559, was meant to serve that reading, as a guide to what a reader should look for in Scripture, never a substitute for it.

What made this more than private scholarship was its setting. Calvin read inside a church, with the fathers constantly at his elbow; Augustine appears on page after page of the Institutes. The Geneva Academy, founded in 1559, trained pastors who carried this disciplined reading into France, Scotland, the Netherlands and, in time, New England. The plain sense, in Calvin's hands, was not a slogan for the untrained. It was a learned discipline exercised for the sake of a congregation.

sections.title: Sola Scriptura and the Answer at Trent
sections.body:
Sola scriptura has become, a way of saying that I need no one but God and my Bible. The Reformers meant something more careful. They held that Scripture is the only infallible rule, the norm that judges every other norm, and that the church's teaching stands under it and can be corrected by it. They did not hold that the creeds, the fathers or the church's long reading were worthless. Luther kept the ecumenical creeds and wrote catechisms. The historian Heiko Oberman distinguished a view in which tradition is the church's faithful interpretation of a sufficient Scripture from a view in which tradition is a second and independent channel of revelation. The Reformers held the first.

The Catholic reply came at the Council of Trent, which in its fourth session, in April 1546, taught that the truth of the gospel is contained in the written books and in the unwritten traditions received from the apostles, and that both are to be received with equal reverence. It declared the Vulgate the approved text for public reading, preaching and disputation, and it forbade anyone, relying on his own judgment, to interpret Scripture against the sense the church has held or against the unanimous consent of the fathers.

Trent deserves its strongest case. The church existed before the New Testament was written, and it was the church that recognized which books belonged to the canon. A Bible does not supply its own table of contents. By 1546 the bishops at Trent had also watched the Reformers divide at Marburg in 1529 over the words of institution, and the radical kingdom at Münster in 1534 and 1535 claim scriptural warrant for polygamy and terror. Their question was fair: if every reader holds the plain sense, who decides when the readers disagree? Protestants have answered it better in some generations than in others. We have not yet made it go away.

sections.title: The Individual Reader and the Debt We Owe
sections.body:
By the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Europe had spent a century and a half fighting over who rightly reads the Bible, and the settlement left the continent divided by confession along borders drawn by princes. Inside those borders the open Bible had done extraordinary good. Ordinary men and women learned to read because they wanted to read Scripture. Catechisms, household prayers and the singing of psalms formed a lay piety more literate and more searching than Europe had known. The conscience of the private Christian acquired a dignity before God that it has never entirely lost, and the long road to religious liberty runs through it.

The culture that printing and the Reformation made also taught Christians to read differently, and not all of the difference was gain. Silent, private reading made the solitary reader the default interpreter. The numbered verse, which Robert Estienne introduced into the New Testament in 1551 and the Geneva Bible carried into English, made Scripture easy to cite and easy to cut apart. The historian Brad Gregory has argued that the Reformation's inability to settle its own disagreements over the plain sense left Western societies with an unresolved pluralism, which they managed by privatizing religion altogether. One need not accept his whole account to feel its sting.

The sting is mine to feel. My own Baptist forebears gave this inheritance a name, soul competency, and E. Y. Mullins made it an axiom of Baptist theology in 1908. There was truth in it, for every person stands before God answerable for himself. But in American hands it slid easily into the conviction that the Bible means whatever it means to me, read alone, without the church, the creeds or the dead. Luther and Calvin would not have recognized it. The plain sense was never meant to be read in an empty room, and we are still learning how much we lost when we emptied it.

keyFigures.name: Johann Gutenberg
keyFigures.note: Mainz printer whose Latin Bible of about 1455 opened the age of the printed book.

keyFigures.name: Desiderius Erasmus
keyFigures.note: Humanist scholar whose Greek New Testament of 1516 let readers check the Vulgate against its source.

keyFigures.name: Martin Luther
keyFigures.note: Wittenberg reformer who set aside the fourfold sense for the grammatical sense and gave Germany its New Testament in 1522.

keyFigures.name: William Tyndale
keyFigures.note: Translator of the English New Testament of 1526, burned at Vilvoorde in 1536, whose phrasing lives on in the King James Version.

keyFigures.name: Thomas More
keyFigures.note: Lord Chancellor and humanist who attacked Tyndale's word choices as an assault on the church's authority.

keyFigures.name: John Calvin
keyFigures.note: Geneva reformer whose commentaries made lucid brevity and the author's intent the interpreter's rule.
